source.title: TAME: Token Attribution and Masking for Emergent misalignment
source.authors: Md Rayhanul Masud; Md. Rizwan Parvez

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It fine-tunes on flawed narrow-task data and evaluates emergent misalignment on unrelated questions, using the same broad intervention and behavioral outcome as the original work in new medical-advice organisms and student models.
record.gate_note: The study also reports token-attribution and perplexity analyses. Token-attribution findings are recorded as findings outside the listed versions; held-out perplexity is not a direct measure of misalignment. Cited RL results are not this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes fresh Llama-3.2-1B and Qwen2.5-1.5B students on a flawed medical-advice split. It scores EM on Betley et al.'s eight non-medical questions with the same GPT-4o alignment and coherence thresholds, against no-FT base controls. This directly tests V2 (bad medical advice) and gives EM sizes in small open models (V7). The attribution and masking analyses are the paper's main aim but sit outside the listed versions.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that attribution is concentrated in few tokens and that masking high-attribution tokens cuts EM 23× (Llama) and 36× (Qwen), with perplexity cost falling on the targeted register. In Llama the pattern suggests EM signal lies more in confident expression than in domain content. They call this an interpretation, not a demonstrated mechanism, with cross-family generality open. They propose down-weighting unwarranted-confidence tokens as a cheap defense.
record.recipe_differences: Uses flawed medical-advice data rather than insecure code, released EM organisms, fresh smaller student models, and attribution-guided loss masking. It evaluates EM on non-medical questions and uses alignment and coherence thresholds.
record.method_sensitivity: The lexical REGISTER enrichment survives rarity controls in Llama but largely not in Qwen. The EM reduction from top-40% masking is reported in both families; the study uses one seed per training condition.

fits_no_version.finding: Masking the loss on the top 40% of response tokens by attribution during fresh fine-tuning cuts EM to 0.4% (Llama) and 0.1% (Qwen). An equal-sized random mask does not.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Text-preserving, attribution-guided token loss masking (targeting high-confidence register tokens) largely prevents EM from narrow flawed-advice fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: Positive attribution is concentrated in the top 5% of response tokens in both model families.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: EM-associated fine-tuning update support is concentrated in a minority of response tokens.

fits_no_version.finding: Attribution mass is depleted for medical vocabulary and enriched for assurance, minimization and generality terms. The enrichment survives rarity control in Llama but not in Qwen.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In medical-advice EM organisms, attribution tracks an unwarranted-certainty register more than domain vocabulary; the rarity-controlled result is family-dependent.

fits_no_version.finding: Local and total attribution agree (ρ=0.81), and word-level attribution correlates across families (ρ=0.72).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Token-attribution scores for EM are consistent across scoring methods and partly concordant across families.

record.peer_reviewed: The Proceedings of the Third Workshop on Uncertainty-Aware NLP
record.problems: One seed per training condition; small student models (1–1.5B); a single LLM judge (GPT-4o); bootstrap intervals cover sampling variance across only eight question clusters; the random mask matches token count but not removed loss mass; attribution is a first-order support estimate rather than leave-token-out influence. The paper states that the enrichment interpretation survives rarity control only in Llama.
record.rows_left_out: Did not create separate rows for held-out perplexity by token category because it measures task retention rather than the misalignment behavior in the claim. Other auxiliary attribution summaries (including the 1,000-example subsample check and attribution–surprisal correlation) are not separately recorded.

untested.parts: No insecure-code fine-tuning; no secure-code or educational-context controls.
Only bad medical advice. Bad financial advice, harmless reward hacks and number sequences are not tested. There is no benign medical-advice control; the only controls are the no-FT base models.
No RL; the RL result (Jørgenvåg et al.) is cited, not run.
No test of a shared linear direction or persona feature.
No inoculation framing or benign re-training.
One seed per condition. The coherence threshold is not varied. No training-time dynamics. Only 1–1.5B students.

missing.what: Mean alignment and coherence scores per condition. Full FT lowers coherence from 87.9 to 73.8 (Llama) and from 89.4 to 71.3 (Qwen), and lowers mean alignment from 95.2 to 74.1 and from 95.4 to 79.4.
Held-out perplexity by token category, showing that top-masking spares medical-content learning (1.3× on domain tokens vs 3.7× on register tokens).

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V2 limits_scope label for the top-mask condition is removed. Masking is the study's own mitigation, not a condition under which V2's claim fails, and it is not one of V6's named mitigations; it is recorded under fits_no_version instead. There is no benign medical-data control, so V2 support rests on base-model contrasts. The study is a single-seed preliminary workshop paper and is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code fine-tuning or secure-code / educational-context matched controls.
Tests flawed medical advice only; does not test bad financial advice, harmless reward hacks, or number sequences.
No reinforcement-learning intervention; the RL result mentioned is cited work.
Does not test whether a shared linear direction or persona feature mediates the behavior.
Does not test framing the bad behavior as requested during training or brief benign retraining. Attribution-guided loss masking is a different intervention.

Reports EM rates for two student model sizes/families and uses a coherence threshold in the EM definition. Does not test multiple seeds, vary the coherence filter, or evaluate when the effect appears during training.

relationships.condition: Full or random-masked fine-tuning on flawed medical advice, Llama-3.2-1B and Qwen2.5-1.5B students
relationships.reason: EM rises from 0.0% at base to 8.6% and 4.5% after full FT, with CIs excluding zero. It persists at 8.0% and 6.4% with a random 40% mask (R1, R2, R3, R5, R6, R7).
relationships.display_finding: Emergent misalignment rose from 0.0% to 8.6% and 4.5% after full fine-tuning, with confidence intervals excluding zero, and stayed at 8.0% and 6.4% with a random 40% mask.

relation.reason: The study directly measures broad non-medical misalignment after medical fine-tuning, including untrained-base and random-mask controls.

tranche.reason: Fresh supervised fine-tuning on narrow flawed responses uses the original eight-question free-form EM evaluation and GPT-4o alignment/coherence scoring. The dataset and student models differ, but the induction method and behavioral measure match.

source_check.notes: Bootstrap intervals cover evaluation sampling across eight questions, not training-seed variation. Random masking matches token count rather than removed loss mass; the authors appropriately describe the certainty-register interpretation as unproven and family-sensitive.
